Two Products

A matrix times its transpose, in two orders: one compares the rows with one another, the other the columns.

A matrix times its transpose, two ways

(XXT)ij=rowi·rowj(XTX)ij=columni·columnj
X with n rows and m columns
productshapecomparesmultiplications
X @ X.Tn × nthe rows: the peoplen · n · m
X.T @ Xm × mthe columns: the genresm · m · n
  • Both symmetric: cell (i, j) equals cell (j, i)
Notes. A matrix times its transpose can be taken in two orders. X times X transposed compares the rows with one another: cell i, j is the dot product of row i and row j. X transposed times X compares the columns. With n rows and m columns the first product is n by n and costs n times n times m multiplications; the second is m by m and costs m times m times n. Both are symmetric. On the movie data the rows are people and the columns are movies or genres, so the two orders answer two questions: how alike are two people, how alike are two movies.

Counts from the rating mask

Bf = B.astype(float)
shared_raters = Bf.T @ Bf      # movies by movies: the people who rated both
shared_movies = Bf @ Bf.T      # people by people: the movies both rated

B.T @ B is 1,297 by 1,297: 1.03 billion multiply-adds, 0.01 s
B @ B.T is 610 by 610: 0.48 billion multiply-adds, 0.00 s
  • B.T @ B: cell (i, j) counts the people who rated both movie i and movie j
  • B @ B.T: the movies that both person i and person j rated
  • 1,297² × 610 ≈ 1.03 billion scalar multiplications; timings shown above
Notes. On the has-rated matrix, 610 people by 1,297 movies. B transposed times B is 1,297 by 1,297: cell i, j counts the people who rated both movies. B times B transposed is 610 by 610: the movies both people rated. The first is a billion multiply-adds, the second half a billion; the printed times are from the laptop that built the deck. B must be numeric first: NumPy's product of Boolean matrices returns True and False, not counts.

Cosine similarity

cos(u,v)=u·v‖u‖‖v‖,S=UTU  with every column of U of length 1
def cosine_of_columns(M):
    lengths = np.linalg.norm(M, axis=0, keepdims=True)
    if np.any(lengths == 0):
        raise ValueError("Cosine similarity is undefined for a zero-length column.")
    U = M / lengths
    return U.T @ U
  • Meeting 10 compared word vectors by the cosine: divide by the lengths, then the dot product
  • Divide every column by its length, and all the cosines at once are one product
Notes. Meeting 10 compared two word vectors by the cosine of the angle between them: the dot product divided by the two lengths. Applied to the columns of a matrix: divide every column by its length, and the cosine of columns i and j is cell i, j of U transposed times U, again one product. The function refuses a column of length zero, for which the cosine is undefined. We will apply this calculation to several representations of the ratings.

Similarity under different rating matrices

the matrixa cell holdswhat cosine compares
B, has-rated1 if the person rated the movierated by the same people
R with 0 in the holesobserved stars, with 0 for missing entrieshigh stars from the same people
Rc, user-centredstars minus the person's mean; 0 in the holesabove or below their usual, together
           has-rated B:  ['Independence Day', 'Jurassic Park', 'Forrest Gump', 'Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope', 'Mission: Impossible', 'Star Wars: Episode VI - Return of the Jedi', 'Toy Story 2']
      ratings as given:  ['Toy Story 2', 'Jurassic Park', 'Independence Day', 'Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope', 'Forrest Gump', 'The Lion King', 'Star Wars: Episode VI - Return of the Jedi']
  user-centred ratings:  ['Toy Story 2', 'Aladdin', 'Toy Story 3', 'Wallace & Gromit: The Wrong Trousers', 'The Incredibles', 'Finding Nemo', 'Blazing Saddles']
Notes. The representation affects the interpretation of cosine similarity. Under B, two movies are similar when the same people rated both: popularity and overlap of raters, not opinion. Zero-filling the raw ratings makes a missing entry numerically identical to a hypothetical zero-star rating. It contributes no dot product term, while each observed rating still affects its column norm. Under the user-centred ratings, every rating has the person's own mean subtracted, and a hole is zero: no deviation from their usual, a modelling choice rather than an opinion. Two ratings above the usual, or two below, add a positive product; opposite deviations a negative one. For Toy Story the three lists differ: shared raters give Independence Day and Jurassic Park; the centred ratings give Toy Story 2, Aladdin, Toy Story 3. The centred list measures agreement in deviations, shared dislikes included, and still depends on which ratings are missing.

Similarities among 40 movies

  • Under B: every cell positive; popular movies share raters; the series have especially high similarities
  • Under Rc: blocks, and blue cells where the same people rate in opposite directions
Notes. The forty most-rated movies, each against each, in the order that makes blocks appear. Under the has-rated matrix every cell is positive: every pair of popular movies shares raters; the series have especially high similarities, because the people who rated one film of a series rated the others. Under the centred ratings the blocks are the series, The Lord of the Rings and Star Wars, and a block of dark films of the 1990s, Pulp Fiction, The Usual Suspects, Fight Club, Seven, Fargo. The blue cells are pairs that the same people rate in opposite directions: Independence Day, Speed and Mission: Impossible against that block. Use the page toggle to compare these similarities with those from the raw ratings.

Products of the word-vector matrix

  • Meeting 10: nearest(word) = U @ v, one row of U @ U.T: 15 million multiplications
  • The full product has 2.5 billion cells: 10 GB in float32 for the output alone
  • U.T @ U, 300 by 300: the dimensions compared with one another
Notes. The word vectors of meeting 10 are a matrix of the same kind: 50,000 words by 300 numbers, every row divided by its length. The diagram shows their relative sizes, with the thinnest dimensions enlarged for visibility. U transposed times U is 300 by 300, the dimensions compared with one another. U times U transposed is 50,000 by 50,000: 2.5 billion cells, 10 gigabytes in float32 for the output alone. This can exceed the available memory, especially with the input and other arrays also present. Meeting 10 never formed it: nearest of a word computed U times one vector, which is one row of that product, 15 million multiplications.

Correlation, similarity and PCA of word vectors

  • Are the 300 dimensions correlated with one another? Z.T @ Z / n, with n = 50,000 words
  • Which words are similar? U @ U.T, one row at a time
  • Along which directions is the cloud of 50,000 words spread out? Act 3
Notes. The same calculations apply to word vectors. The correlation of the 300 dimensions is a 300 by 300 product over 50,000 words. The similarity of words is the big product, taken a row at a time. And the directions along which the word cloud is spread are the subject of Act 3. Ask the class what they expect for the word vectors. The talking points give measured results.
